label: What Is Curvature
notes: This opening chapter, printed pages one through eight, is purely motivational. Lee asks a single question before any machinery appears: what does it mean for a space to be curved? We preview the three classical problems that historically forced mathematicians to make curvature precise and quantitative.

label: Three Classical Problems
notes: Curvature did not arrive as a definition; it emerged from three problems. The parallel postulate and non-Euclidean geometry, the curvature of plane curves and surfaces, and the deep link between curvature and topology each demanded a measurable notion of bending that this chapter introduces informally.

label: The Parallel Postulate
notes: Euclid's fifth postulate resisted proof for two thousand years. Attempts to derive it failed because consistent geometries exist where it is false. Replacing it yields spherical geometry with no parallels and hyperbolic geometry with many, and curvature is precisely what distinguishes these alternatives.

label: Curvature of a Plane Curve
notes: For a plane curve the curvature measures how fast the unit tangent turns with arc length. A straight line never turns, so its curvature is zero. A tight bend turns quickly, giving large curvature, which we now make precise through the best-fitting circle at each point.

label: The Osculating Circle
notes: At a point of a curve there is a unique circle that matches position, tangent direction, and second-order bending. This osculating circle has radius R, the radius of curvature. Its reciprocal one over R measures how sharply the curve bends, independent of how we parametrize the curve.

label: Kappa Equals One Over R
notes: The signed curvature kappa equals one over the radius of the osculating circle. Large radius means gentle bending and small kappa; small radius means a sharp turn and large kappa. This single scalar captures everything about second-order shape for a plane curve.

label: From Curves to Surfaces
notes: On a surface curvature becomes richer because we may slice in many directions. Each normal plane cuts out a plane curve with its own curvature. The principal curvatures are the extreme values among all these normal sections, and their product defines the Gaussian curvature of the surface.

label: Gaussian Curvature
notes: Gauss defined the curvature of a surface as the product of the two principal curvatures, kappa one times kappa two. Its sign classifies local shape: positive where the surface is dome-like, negative where it is saddle-like, and zero where one principal direction stays flat.

label: The Sign of Curvature
notes: Three model surfaces fix intuition. The sphere bends the same way in every direction and has positive Gaussian curvature. The flat plane has zero curvature everywhere. The saddle bends oppositely in two directions, so the product of principal curvatures is negative.

label: Theorema Egregium
notes: Gauss's remarkable theorem states that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic: it can be computed from measurements made entirely within the surface, with no reference to the surrounding space. Bending paper preserves it, which is why a flat sheet cannot wrap a sphere without distortion.

label: Curvature and Topology
notes: The Gauss-Bonnet theorem ties total curvature to topology: integrating Gaussian curvature over a closed surface gives two pi times its Euler characteristic. Local bending and global shape are therefore inseparable, the third classical problem that motivates the whole subject.

label: Generalizing to Manifolds
notes: The book's program is to lift these surface ideas to Riemannian manifolds of any dimension. A metric measures lengths and angles, geodesics generalize straight lines, and the Riemann curvature tensor encodes in higher dimensions exactly what Gaussian curvature captured for surfaces.
